title: Clauses
subtitle: Relative, participle, infinitive and concession clauses

rows.use: who · people (and animals when we want to give them a personality)
rows.example: There are a lot of people **who** hate having injections.

rows.use: which · things and concepts (and animals when we don't want to give them a personality)
rows.example: This is the prescription **which** the doctor gave me.

rows.use: whom · people (as an object; must be used directly after a preposition)
rows.example: That's the consultant **with whom** I spoke.

rows.use: that · a more informal word for who, which, when, where, why; only used in defining relative clauses
rows.example: This is the prescription **that** the doctor gave me.
I'll never forget the day **when** I broke my finger.

rows.use: where · place or situation; = in/at/etc which
rows.example: Harley Street, **where** she was born, is famous for its clinics.

rows.use: why · often after the word reason; = the reason for which; only used in defining relative clauses
rows.example: And that's (the reason) **why** I wanted to become a vet.

rows.use: whose · the possessive of who and which; can also come after a preposition
rows.example: There are several kids in my class **whose** parents are doctors.

rows.use: what · the thing(s) which; only used in defining relative clauses
rows.example: **What** I don't understand is why she didn't take her pills.

blocks.text: When we use a preposition with a relative pronoun, it is more formal to put the preposition before the pronoun.
blocks.note: This is the medical encyclopaedia **to which** I referred. (very formal) · This is the medical encyclopaedia **which I referred to**. (less formal)

blocks.text: **Which** can refer to the whole preceding clause, rather than just the preceding noun.
blocks.note: She announced that she wanted to be a pathologist, **which** really shocked us. (= the announcement shocked us)

blocks.text: **Defining relative clauses** tell us which one of a group of things/people we are talking about. The sentence doesn't usually make complete sense if we remove the relative clause. **Non-defining relative clauses** simply give us more information about someone/something. The sentence makes complete sense if we remove the relative clause.

rows.example: That's the doctor **who did Karen's operation**. · That's the doctor **that did Karen's operation**. (more informal)
Dr Lake, **who has been working here for over ten years**, is a very experienced surgeon.

rows.use: Defining · no comma; object pronoun can be omitted
rows.example: That's the doctor **who she saw**. (more formal) · That's the doctor **she saw**. (less formal)
Dr Lake, **who is my uncle**, is 50 years old.

rows.use: Defining · when, where and why can be omitted
rows.example: I'll never forget the day **when I broke my arm**. · I'll never forget the day **I broke my arm**.

rows.use: Non-defining · cannot omit where and when
rows.example: Harley Street, **where she was born**, is famous for its clinics.
We cannot put a number or a determiner such as **some, none, much** and **many** before **of which** or **of whom** in a defining clause.
I bought some drugs, **some of which** were expensive.
She was the nurse **looking** after the patients at the time. (who was looking) · The boy **taken** to hospital was 13 years old. (who was taken)
After **giving** blood, I went home. · After **having given** blood, I went home.

rows.use: To explain the reason for something
rows.example: **Being** frightened of needles, Tony was not looking forward to the injection.

rows.use: To talk about actions happening at the same time
rows.example: **Sitting** in the waiting room, I could hear the sound of the dentist's drill.

rows.use: To talk about actions happening in sequence
rows.example: **Having found** an optician close to the office, I made an appointment for that evening.
**Given** an aspirin, I began to feel better. (when/because I was given an aspirin)
**Given** the chance, I'd definitely study pharmacology. (If I were given the chance)

blocks.text: When the participle clause doesn't have its own subject, the clause and the rest of the sentence must both refer to the same subject.
blocks.note: **Standing** in the hot, crowded room, I began to feel dizzy. (= I was standing) · Standing in the hot, crowded room, **my head** began to feel heavy. (incorrect: my head wasn't standing)

rows.example: **To be** a successful surgeon is the dream of many young children. (= It is the dream of many young children to be a successful surgeon.)
My job is **to give** the patients their lunch.
**Even though** she'd put on sun cream, Tamsin got burnt. · Tamsin got burnt, **though** she had put on sun cream. · Tamsin put on sun cream. She still got burnt, **though**.

rows.use: in spite of / despite (+ noun or -ing)
rows.example: **Despite** putting on sun cream, Tamsin got burnt. · **In spite of the fact that** she put on sun cream, Tamsin got burnt. · **Despite the** sun cream, Tamsin still got burnt.
**While** antibiotics are effective against bacteria, they do not work against viruses. · Bacterial infections can be cured with antibiotics, **whereas** viruses cannot.

Penicillin is a powerful antibiotic. **However**, some people are allergic to it. · Penicillin is a powerful antibiotic. Some people are allergic to it, **however**. · Penicillin is a powerful antibiotic. Some people, **however**, are allergic to it.

**Try as he might**, he couldn't put up with the pain. · **However hard he (might have) tried**, he couldn't put up with the pain. · **Hard though/as he tried**, he couldn't put up with the pain. · **Much as he tried**, he couldn't put up with the pain.

blocks.text: With **in spite of / despite + -ing**, both parts of the sentence must refer to the same subject.

**Even if** is used to emphasise that it doesn't matter if something happens or is true, another situation remains the same. **Even if** is also used to suggest that something may or may not happen, **whereas even though** suggests that the action actually takes place.
blocks.note: **Even if** they found a cure for cancer tomorrow, it would take several years before it was available. · **Even if** she tried to give her an injection, she couldn't. (= She probably hasn't tried yet.) · **Even though** she tried to give her an injection, she couldn't. (= She tried and was unsuccessful.)

exercises.title: A · Relative pronouns
exercises.instruction: Write a relative pronoun in each gap. Do not use the word that.

items.prompt: Davina, ___ kids you met last weekend, works for Cooper's in the high street.
I'll never understand the reason ___ you decided to join the army.
The village ___ Alan grew up in is only a few miles from here.
Have you spoken to that guy ___ daughter might be able to help you with the contract?
Back in the 1970s, ___ I was a teenager, no one I knew had a computer.
They've just announced that Beddington youth club, ___ we all used to hang out after school, is going to be turned into a casino.
Chicago's a city ___ I've always wanted to visit.
Do you remember the time ___ we got totally lost?
The cows ___ are in that field over there are Friesians.
Our cat Tibby, ___ loves being stroked all the time, is 16 years old today!

___ spoils the film for me is the ending, which is just ridiculous.

exercises.title: B · Which can be replaced by that?
exercises.instruction: For each sentence from A, choose whether the relative pronoun you used can be replaced by that.

Back in the 1970s, when I was a teenager … Can when be replaced by that?
items.explanation: This is a non-defining time clause, so that is not possible.
